races.title: 11th Congressional District
races.fullText:
On paper, Democrats shouldn’t have much shot at winning the state’s westernmost U.S. House seat. President Donald Trump carried the district by 9.5 percentage points in 2024, and Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards won it by 13.5 points the same year. 

But this year has been far from normal. Edwards abandoned his re-election bid in August after a House ethics panel concluded that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” The House then voted nearly unanimously to censure him.

The move set off a frenzy among Republicans to find someone to replace him on the ballot. Ultimately, local party leaders tapped state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom of Henderson County.

Democratic farmer Jamie Ager has enjoyed widespread support within his party, with national groups stepping in to back him even before the primary was over. Ager enters the fall with months of campaign trail experience that Balkcom doesn’t have, and his Hickory Nut Gap Farms is well-known in the region.

Meanwhile, Balkcom’s state House district only covers northern Henderson County. While she has given media interviews and appeared at a rally alongside Trump to try to boost her name recognition, it could be difficult to overcome her late start.

Balkcom won’t report her first fundraising numbers until mid-October, but Ager had a big head start there, too. He entered July with nearly $2.2 million in his campaign coffers, which goes a long way in the Asheville media market.

In ads, both candidates have tried to out-folksy the other, with Ager highlighting the monthly barn dances at his farm and Balkcom emphasizing her family’s “tough mountain leadership” with a story about the time her mother shot a home intruder.

In June 2025, The Assembly reported that most local observers agreed that Republicans were favored to hold this seat. But as of early October, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considers this race a toss-up.

races.title: 1st Congressional District
races.fullText:
When Trump encouraged states to redraw district maps mid-decade to bolster Republican chances of preserving their U.S. House majority, North Carolina state Senate leader Phil Berger quickly obliged. Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis was the main target.

This year’s contest is a rematch of the 2024 battle between Davis and Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout. In that race, Davis edged out Buckhout by 1.7 percentage points. After redistricting, the 1st District is 6 points more favorable to Republicans; it swung for Trump by 7.3 points in 2020 and 11.6 points in 2024.

All that to say: Davis has his work cut out for him. But he’s repeatedly proven he shouldn’t be underestimated. He’s bucked his party on tough votes, most recently by supporting a resolution condemning socialism. During his time in the state legislature, he defied then-Gov. Roy Cooper on votes like increased restrictions on abortion.

Buckhout has said she didn’t expect to enter this race. She initially supported Rocky Mount Mayor Sandy Roberson, who backed out as his city faced a financial crisis. Buckhout then fended off Carteret County Sheriff Asa Buck and now-former state Sen. Bobby Hanig for the GOP nomination.

Cook Political Report recently changed its rating to show this race is a toss-up. Voters are frustrated with rising costs of living, and Trump’s approval ratings remain low, so this is one to watch.

races.title: Senate District 11
races.fullText:
For a read on the mood of the state, look no further than the Nash County district held by Republican state Sen. Lisa Stone Barnes.

Barnes has flooded the airwaves, a sign that Republicans see this as a critical battleground. She faces a formidable opponent in James Gailliard, a pastor and former member of the state House. The two briefly overlapped in the chamber.

Gailliard is campaigning as someone who won’t rubberstamp his party’s priorities. He bucked then-Gov. Cooper on issues like abortion. Despite his independent streak, Gailliard has said he wouldn’t override any of Gov. Josh Stein’s vetoes if elected.

Barnes has consistently stuck with the GOP on contentious issues this legislative session.

To break the Republican supermajority in the state Senate, Democrats need all their incumbents to win and to pick off one GOP seat. Barnes won re-election in 2024 by less than 2.6 points, the closest Senate race a Republican won that cycle. This district could present Democrats with their best pickup opportunity.

races.title: State Supreme Court
races.fullText:
This statewide contest won’t change much about the current court, but it’s key in the long run.

If Democratic Justice Anita Earls wins re-election, the high court would maintain the 5-2 conservative advantage. But it would put Democrats in a better position to flip the court in 2028, when three Republican seats are on the ballot.

That matters because the legislature will draw new voting maps after the 2030 U.S. Census, and the court could wind up having to weigh in—which would have a big impact on the 2032 election.

If Earls loses to former state Rep. Sarah Stevens, Republicans would gain a 6-1 advantage on the Supreme Court. The differences between Earls and Stevens also couldn’t be starker. Stevens could wind up assessing the constitutionality of bills she voted on; she’s already signaled it would take a lot to get her to strike down state laws.

Earls, meanwhile, routinely issues scathing dissents and pushes for changes to the legal system. Earls co-chaired a racial equity task force under Cooper, which Stevens viewed as mixing the responsibilities of the executive and judicial branches.

Earls’ campaign entered July with 13 times the cash on hand as Stevens. While Stevens has been elusive on the campaign trail, Earls has held or attended roughly 200 public or campaign events in the past year.

Two years ago, the state Supreme Court race was a nail-biter that dragged on for months amid legal challenges. This contest may not turn out to be that close, but it checks the boxes for consequential and interesting.

races.title: U.S. Senate
races.fullText:
The placement for this race provoked the most debate at The Assembly, and readers could argue this contest should be either a lot higher or a lot lower on this list.

On one hand, it’s no longer expected to be very competitive. Real Clear Polling shows Cooper up by an average of 9 points over Republican Michael Whatley in surveys in September. On the other hand, if Democrats take control of the U.S. Senate, it could carry important ramifications for the last two years of Trump’s presidency, particularly if there are any vacancies to fill on the U.S. Supreme Court.

Democrats haven’t won a Senate seat in North Carolina since 2008. And if this race is decided by double digits, as some polls show as a possibility, it’d be the worst outcome for a Republican Senate candidate in this state since 1974. Less clear is whether that would have any meaningful impact on down-ballot races. Lt. Gov. Mark Robinson’s historically bad performance in the 2024 gubernatorial race didn’t seem to dissuade Republican voters from supporting GOP candidates lower on the ballot.

Cooper has never lost an election in his nearly 40 years in politics. Whatley is a first-time candidate who has made a handful of rookie mistakes. He has also stuck close to Trump, who tapped him to lead the Republican National Committee and effectively anointed him as the GOP nominee in this race.

Whatley also has been unusually selective in his media strategy for a candidate who isn’t well-known to voters. He’s largely stuck to interviews with conservative television, talk radio, and websites rather than nonpartisan news outlets. It’s also likely to be the first time in almost 30 years the two major party candidates haven’t debated.

Earlier this month, the Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s top super PAC for bolstering Senate candidates, pulled N.C. advertising to prioritize Kansas, Semafor reported. A Whatley campaign official also told The News & Observer it has paused TV ads and is reevaluating its messaging strategy.

While there’s always the possibility of some wild October surprise, that seems highly unlikely to happen to Cooper, who has been in the public spotlight since his first run for public office in 1986.

races.title: House District 25
races.fullText:
Republicans are one seat shy of a supermajority in the state House. Democrats, meanwhile, would need to flip a dozen seats to take control of the chamber.

That would take a major blue wave, but it’s not impossible. One place to watch is the Nash County seat held by GOP state Rep. Allen Chesser. This is a rematch of the 2024 battle between the incumbent and Democrat Lorenza Wilkins, a youth center co-founder who previously worked in human resources for the city of Rocky Mount.

In 2024, this race was one of a handful within the recount threshold. Given the national mood, Chesser seems more vulnerable this year.

But Democrats haven’t made Wilkins their top priority. Wilkins isn’t one of the 14 legislative races the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee is tracking in N.C. Even so, he entered the summer on a decent financial footing, with $136,000 in available cash to Chesser’s $116,000.

races.title: House District 37
races.fullText:
Republican state Rep. Erin Paré of Wake County has steadily climbed up the party’s political ladder since taking office in 2021.

While she’s not in leadership, she has a lot of influence within the chamber as one of three vice chairs of the Rules Committee, which often determines bills’ chances of success.

As a co-chair of the House Appropriations Committee, she pushed for substantial pay increases for starting teachers. But she’s come under fire locally for wading into social issues, including the hiring of a transgender public school teacher.

Paré is running against Winn Decker, an education policy consultant and former deputy director for higher education at the Hunt Institute. 

Decker is campaigning on reining in electricity costs and bolstering public education spending. He also told The News & Observer that he opposes the proposed merger between WakeMed and Atrium health systems. 

Democrats have Paré among their top political targets this year, but she has a track record of winning competitive races and outperforming other Republicans. This contest will also be one of the most expensive due to the cost of ads in Raleigh’s media market.

races.title: House District 35
races.fullText:
Republican state Rep. Mike Schietzelt of Wake County is perhaps the most beloved, accessible, and vulnerable freshman in his caucus. 

He fought off a proposal for toll roads along Raleigh’s Capital Boulevard and sponsored eight bills that have become law, including one opting the state into Trump’s school voucher initiative. 

His re-election campaign is a rematch against Democrat Evonne Hopkins, a family law attorney he defeated by 3.2 points in 2024. 

Republicans have criticized Hopkins’ comments about Flock cameras at a candidate forum last month. “I have literally caught people cheating on their spouses by accessing this data,” she said. “That’s how readily available the information about you is.”

Republicans suggested she admitted to unlawfully accessing private data. In a statement to The Assembly, Hopkins said she didn’t break the law. “My point at the forum was about privacy: The amount of access to vehicular and personal information this technology allows should concern all of us,” she said. “I will not discuss the details of a client’s case to satisfy a political attack.”

Schietzelt has stuck with the GOP majority in all but one of the 784 votes taken thus far.

races.title: Senate District 7
races.fullText:
If there is one lawmaker Democrats most want out of office, it’s Republican state Sen. Michael Lee of New Hanover County. He’s one of four senators who have thrown their names in the hat to succeed Berger as Senate leader, but the only one running in a competitive district.

Lee has been in the General Assembly since 2014, except for a two-year gap after losing in 2018. He’s steadily ascended the GOP ranks and has major influence over education policy as a staunch supporter of the private school voucher program.

Lee’s district has been redrawn several times to make it less favorable for Democrats. He won re-election in 2022 by less than 2 points, but after redistricting in 2024, he carried the district by 8.5 points.

Still, if Democratic challenger Jessica Bichler beats expectations or pulls off an upset, that could shake up the brewing Senate GOP leadership battle, so political insiders are watching this one closely.

races.title: Senate District 18
races.fullText:
If Democrats are going to break the state Senate supermajority, they likely can’t lose this district.

This Wake County contest was the most competitive among the 170 state legislative races in 2024, with Democrat Terence Everitt winning by a mere 0.11 percentage points, or 128 votes.

Everitt resigned from the legislature earlier this year, and Wake Forest Commissioner Haseeb Fatmi took his place. While Fatmi is technically running as an incumbent, that’s not how the race feels. Wake Forest accounts for just 22% of the district’s population, which means he’s had less than six months to introduce himself to 154,000 new constituents.

His Republican opponent, Chris Stock, won handily in a contentious primary, thanks in part to his frequent in-person campaigning. Stock also lives in Wake Forest.

Fatmi may have a slight edge, but this race is still likely to be close.

races.title: House District 74
races.fullText:
There was no bigger missed opportunity for Democrats in 2024 than the Forsyth County seat held by Republican Rep. Jeff Zenger. 

At the time, the party prioritized protecting Democratic incumbents over taking down Republicans in similar districts. That was probably a mistake: Democrat Amy Taylor North outperformed those incumbents, losing by less than 4 points.

State Democratic party leaders appear to have learned a lesson. 

Taylor North, a small business owner, should be able to make up some ground in a more favorable environment for her party this year. Whether it’ll be enough for her to edge out Zenger in this rematch remains to be seen.

races.title: Senate District 34
races.fullText:
Republicans in Cabarrus County are deeply fractured, presenting Democrats with an opportunity to pick up a seat. 

Republican Kevin Crutchfield has found himself in competitive primaries in three runs for legislative office. He won a state House seat in 2022, then narrowly lost his re-election bid to GOP challenger Brian Echevarria. This year, Crutchfield set his sights on the Senate, sensing a vulnerability in Chris Measmer, whom Republicans appointed to fill the seat Paul Newton vacated in 2025.

Crutchfield narrowly edged out Measmer, but the win left a sour taste in the mouths of some of his fellow Republicans. 

Now Democrat April Cook, a co-founder of a health clinic, is looking to capitalize on that discontent. On paper, Democrats should lose this race. Newton won by 9 percentage points in 2024, but Crutchfield is neither in party leadership nor a state Senate veteran. In a bad election cycle for Republicans, this seat could provide a good read on the mood of the electorate.

races.title: House District 105
races.fullText:
On the House side, Democrats have concentrated a lot of their attention on state Rep. Tricia Cotham of Mecklenburg County.

She drew their ire in 2023 after switching her political party affiliation and giving House Republicans a supermajority. GOP leadership rewarded her by redistricting her seat from safely Democratic to lean-Republican.

It worked, at least temporarily. Cotham fended off a Democratic challenger in 2024 by 0.4 percentage points—213 votes—the narrowest margin of victory for any GOP incumbent. Of all the Republicans on the ballot this year, she’s seen as the most vulnerable. She’s also dealt with health issues that kept her off the campaign trail, including major jaw surgery.

This year, she faces a challenge from Ken McCool, a lifelong Matthews resident and former town commissioner who runs a sports cards and collectibles store.

With motivated Democrats and Republicans facing a tough national climate, Cotham could be in deep trouble.

races.title: Court of Appeals
races.fullText:
Historically, all statewide judicial candidates perform similarly, so we’re bundling the three Court of Appeals races into one for this list.

These aren’t the sexiest races by any means, but they are among the most important, as these judges often hear contentious political and policy matters.

All three seats up for grabs this year are currently held by Democrats, so this year isn’t going to reduce the GOP’s 12-3 majority.

Democratic incumbents John Arrowood and Toby Hampson are squaring off against Republicans Michael Byrne and George Cooper Bell. In an open Democratic seat, Christine Marie Walczyk faces Republican Craig Collins.

races.title: House District 32
races.fullText:
It’s been quite the political journey for Democratic state Rep. Bryan Cohn of Granville County. He passed on a re-election bid this year, only to find himself sucked back in after his potential successor pulled out of the race for health reasons.

Now, Cohn is squaring off against Republican Frank Sossamon in a rematch of 2024, when Cohn won by a mere 0.5 points—228 votes. Cohn has bucked his party and Gov. Josh Stein at times, most notably on an electricity bill that did away with a carbon reduction goal. That hasn’t made him the most-liked member of his caucus.

Nevertheless, he has a track record of electoral success. Even in a tough environment, Republicans see an opportunity to get Sossamon, a former House member himself, back into office. If any House Democrats are going to lose this year, Cohn is certainly among the most vulnerable.

races.title: Senate District 42
races.fullText:
Woodson Bradley, meanwhile, is the most vulnerable incumbent Democrat in the state Senate. In 2024, she won by a mere 209 votes, or 0.16 points. And once again, she’ll be going toe-to-toe with GOP attorney Stacie McGinn.

McGinn, a former Bank of America executive, exceeded expectations in 2024 in what had been a lean-Democratic seat in southeast Mecklenburg County previously held by Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt. McGinn has renewed her concerns over Bradley’s past work as a top salesperson for Fortune Hi-Tech Marketing, a company the Federal Trade Commission shut down and law enforcement officials labeled as a massive pyramid scheme. Bradley maintains she was a victim, not a perpetrator.

races.title: House District 24
races.fullText:
Democratic Rep. Dante Pittman of Wilson County is a divisive figure within his party. Given the nature of his swing district, he must walk a political tightrope to assert his independence without  alienating the party base.

Nowhere was that tension clearer than when he supported a law requiring public school districts to publish a list of available books. The measure lets parents block their children from borrowing specific books and allows them to cite their religious beliefs to remove their child from activities and discussions. Pittman backed the bill initially but then opposed overriding Stein’s veto. He said his opinion changed when he learned that a provision preventing public funds from being used for youth gender transition procedures was already part of a 2023 law. 

Pittman has secured a number of priorities for the district, including $12 million for Wilson Community College to build a biologics training center, $500,000 for Barton College’s nursing and primary care program, and $440,000 for a volunteer fire department.

His GOP challenger, Blake Boykin, chairs the Wilson County Board of Education.

The district is as swingy as it gets, having flip-flopped between Democrats and Republicans in each of the last three elections. While Pittman is the favorite, victory is not assured.

races.title: House District 115
races.fullText:
Democratic Rep. Lindsey Prather’s Buncombe County district was redrawn in 2024 to lean Republican. After Hurricane Helene devastated the region weeks before the election, she was on the ground aggressively pushing for recovery funds.

Prather’s re-election gave Democrats the seat they needed to break the Republican supermajority. She continues to be a thorn in the side of GOP leaders on Helene recovery, and the slow pace of funding has frustrated Democrats and Republicans alike in Western N.C. That could hurt the party in power, or it could mean voters want a fresh face.

Her Republican challenger, Swannanoa Fire Chief Anthony Penland, raised more than $20,000 from individuals in the first half of the year, suggesting he’s got some local support.

Still, he faces a tall task in trying to unseat Prather, who entered July with seven times more cash at her disposal.

races.title: Senate District 4
races.fullText:
This race comes with a personal disclaimer: Jess Rivera, the Democrat trying to oust Republican incumbent Buck Newton, is my barber, so I haven’t covered this race. That said, I’m keeping an eye on it. 

For Democrats to even get to a 25-25 split in the Senate, they’d need to hold onto all their existing seats and net an additional five. This district would be a must-have.

Newton won by double digits in 2024, and the map hasn’t changed. Even so, it’s one of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee’s 14 targets, suggesting they see some window of opportunity for Rivera, a Marine veteran, and are putting money into her race.

races.title: House District 63
races.fullText:
This selection may come as a bit of a surprise, as Alamance County hasn’t elected a Democrat to the legislature since 2020, when Democrat Ricky Hurtado defeated Republican Stephen Ross by 1 point.

But that victory was an anomaly, as Republicans were forced to redraw the legislative map that year to comply with a court order. Since then, North Carolina’s conservative majority on the state Supreme Court has allowed the legislature to draw maps that benefit the GOP.

Ross narrowly defeated Hurtado in a 2022 rematch and won in 2024 by double digits. This year, he declined to seek re-election, paving the way for attorney Ryan Moffitt.

Democrat Ian Baltutis has other plans. As the former mayor of Burlington, the county’s largest city, he’s had ample opportunity to get to know voters, though he’s been out of office since 2021.

This race is also a battle between two Elon alums: Baltutis graduated in 2008 with a business degree, and Moffitt graduated from the Elon University School of Law in 2014.

As an Elon alum, I’m watching this race with great curiosity. While it’s a bit of a longshot for Democrats on paper, the absence of an incumbent has cracked open the door.

races.title: House District 73
races.fullText:
Democrats spent heavily last cycle in an unsuccessful effort to hold the seat of then-Rep. Diamond Staton-Williams of Cabarrus County, who lost to Republican Jonathan Almond by 6 points. This year, Republicans are the ones on defense, and the Cabarrus GOP is as fractured as any county party.

If Republican antipathy trickles down the ballot, Democrat Thomas Monks could pull off a major upset. But his fundraising numbers are abysmal–a mere $7,000 raised since the start of his campaign. The race isn’t the biggest priority for Democrats, and money is most certainly on the GOP side.

Still, this is a district that should be in play.

races.title: House District 5
races.fullText:
Astonishingly, both candidates in this race have raised almost nothing, despite it being a major political battleground on paper. Republican incumbent Bill Ward of Pasquotank County received only two individual contributions in the first half of the year, while Democratic challenger Sam Davis III has raised little more than $3,000 this entire election cycle. 

In the 2022 midterms, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Cheri Beasley carried the district by 6 points. That same year, Ward carried it by almost 8. This sizable gap is pretty unusual and indicates that Democrats could win here with the right candidate.

Whether Davis’ fresh face will appeal to voters isn’t certain. But in the absence of substantial outside support in the closing weeks of the election, Ward could coast to victory.

races.title: House District 64
races.fullText:
Folks may be surprised to learn Republican Rep. Dennis Riddell is on the airwaves in Alamance County this year. He faces the same Democratic opponent he did in 2024, LeVon Barnes, whom he defeated by nearly 10 points.

Could this time be different? There’s some reason to think so. Both Riddell and Barnes raised $21,000 from mid-February through June. 

Behind the scenes, the progressive political group Work for Democracy has helped prop up Barnes. Party activists have also taken to social media to blast Riddell over his opposition to raising the minimum wage. While the anti-Riddell messaging has gotten a good amount of traction online, we’ll learn whether that translates into votes.

races.title: House District 82
races.fullText:
The House Democratic Caucus has amped up its online campaign to unseat Republican Rep. Brian Echevarria of Cabarrus County by resurfacing social media posts in which he wrote about how he is keen on “sexually harassing” his wife.

Echevarria is among the most vocal members of his caucus and ruffled some feathers when he unseated the incumbent Crutchfield in the 2024 state House primary. Lingering frustrations could hurt Crutchfield’s Senate campaign and Echevarria’s attempt to hold onto his seat.

While Echevarria hasn’t raised much money this year, he entered July with more than $90,000 in his coffers. His Democratic opponent, Chris Bishopp, has outraised Echevarria by a 4-to-1 margin, which indicates there’s some momentum.

races.title: House District 20
races.fullText:
State Rep. Ted Davis of New Hanover County isn’t seeking re-election this year, and county commissioner Dane Scalise is looking to keep the seat under GOP control.

He’ll have to fend off Democrat Tim Merrick. The House Republican Caucus has launched an advertising campaign against Merrick and taken to social media to amplify an article in which he was quoted after the 9/11 terrorist attacks as saying, “We have not been fair to nations in the Middle East.”

The attention Republicans are paying to this race suggests they see Merrick as a threat. Even so, Davis carried the seat by 12 points, and Scalise remains the strong favorite.

races.title: Senate District 26
races.fullText:
It only seems appropriate to round out the Top 26 with Senate District 26. If it sounds familiar, it was our No. 1 primary to watch in the spring and far and away the most expensive. Senate leader Phil Berger fell short to a challenge from former Rockingham County Sheriff Sam Page.

Needless to say, the race left a sour taste in the mouths of GOP leadership, and it might turn some voters off Page.

Berger defeated Democrat Steve Luking in the 2024 general election by 13 points. Page has nowhere near the same resources at his disposal, as he spent so much in his quest to claim the Republican nomination.

Luking has made a number of inroads for Democrats here. He held positions at Annie Penn Hospital in Reidsville, is a longtime Sierra Club member, and has also served on the Rockingham County Board of Health.

Perhaps most notable: He entered July with more than $54,000 in the bank to Page’s $17,000. As we learned from the Page-Berger primary, money can’t buy elections. But the fundraising does show Luking may have more support than Republicans are anticipating.

While a Page defeat would be a colossal upset, voters have shown they can surprise folks. Plus, when Page is involved, you can’t help but watch.
